python3 << 'EOF'
from PIL import Image
import numpy as np

im = Image.open('barcode.png')
print('mode:', im.mode, 'size:', im.size)
a = np.array(im.convert('RGB')).astype(float)
h, w, _ = a.shape
print('shape:', a.shape)

# Check for color: max channel spread
spread = np.abs(a[...,0] - a[...,1]) + np.abs(a[...,1] - a[...,2])
print('max channel spread:', spread.max(), 'mean:', spread.mean())

lum = a.mean(axis=2)  # h x w
colmean = lum.mean(axis=0)  # w

# Detect stripe width: find columns that are identical to neighbors
diff = np.abs(np.diff(colmean))
print('col-to-col diff: max', diff.max(), 'mean', diff.mean())

# columns that are exactly identical to previous column (same stripe)
same = np.all(np.abs(np.diff(lum, axis=1)) < 1e-9, axis=0)
# count runs
runs = []
cur = 1
for i in range(1, w):
    if same[i-1]:
        cur += 1
    else:
        runs.append(cur); cur = 1
runs.append(cur)
print('num runs (stripes):', len(runs))
vals, counts = np.unique(runs, return_counts=True)
print('run-length histogram:', dict(zip(vals.tolist(), counts.tolist())))

print('overall mean lum:', lum.mean())
print('percent dark cols (<40):', (colmean<40).mean())
print('percent bright cols (>200):', (colmean>200).mean())
EOF

from PIL import Image
import numpy as np

a = np.array(Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')).astype(float)
lum = a.mean(axis=2)
col = lum.mean(axis=0)  # 1000 stripe means

print('min', col.min(), 'max', col.max(), 'mean', col.mean(), 'median', np.median(col))
for t in [10,20,40,60,80,100,120,150,180,200]:
    print(f'frac < {t}: {(col<t).mean():.3f}   frac > {t}: {(col>t).mean():.3f}')

# Coarse profile: 40 bins of 25 stripes, show as sparkline-ish
bins = np.array_split(col, 40)
prof = np.array([b.mean() for b in bins])
print('\n40-bin profile (each bin = 25 stripes = 2.5% of movie):')
for i,p in enumerate(prof):
    n = int(p/4)
    print(f'{i*2.5:5.1f}%  {p:6.1f}  ' + '#'*n)
EOF

That's a strong clue — several candidates (Joan of Arc, His Girl Friday, The Lady Vanishes, The Kid) are high-key bright films and are unlikely. # Std of profile = contrast of the time series
print('\nprofile std:', prof.std().round(1))

***The Last Man on Earth*** ([Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language"): ***L'ultimo uomo della Terra***) is a 1964 [post-apocalyptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocalyptic_and_post-apocalyptic_fiction "Apocalyptic and post-apocalyptic fiction") [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction_film "Science fiction film") [horror film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_film "Horror film") directed by [Sidney Salkow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Salkow "Sidney Salkow") and [Ubaldo Ragona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubaldo_Ragona "Ubaldo Ragona"), based on the 1954 novel *[I Am Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Legend_\(novel\) "I Am Legend (novel)")* by [Richard Matheson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Matheson "Richard Matheson"). It stars [Vincent Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Price "Vincent Price") and [Franca Bettoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franca_Bettoia "Franca Bettoia"), and was produced by [Robert L. Lippert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_L._Lippert "Robert L. Lippert"). The screenplay was written in part by Matheson, but he was dissatisfied with the result and chose to be credited under the alias "Logan Swanson".

The film was a co-production between the United States and Italy, and was filmed on-location in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"). It was released in the United States by [American International Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_International_Pictures "American International Pictures"). In the 1980s, the film entered the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain").[\[1\]](#cite_note-2)[\[2\]](#cite_note-3)

*The Last Man on Earth* is the first of three adaptations of Matheson's novel, followed by *[The Omega Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Omega_Man "The Omega Man")* (1971) and [*I Am Legend*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Legend_\(film\) "I Am Legend (film)") (2007).

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*The Last Man on Earth* (full movie)

It is 1968, and Dr. Robert Morgan lives in a world where everyone else has been infected by a [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemic "Pandemic") that has turned them into [undead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undead "Undead"), [vampiric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire") creatures that cannot stand sunlight, fear mirrors, and are repelled by [garlic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic "Garlic"). They would kill Morgan if they could, but they are weak and unintelligent. Every day Morgan carries out the same routine: He wakes up, marks another day on the calendar, gathers his weapons, and then goes hunting for [vampires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire"), killing as many as he can and then burning the bodies to prevent them from coming back. At night, he locks himself inside his house.

A [flashback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashback_\(narrative\) "Flashback (narrative)") sequence explains that, in December 1965, Morgan's wife Virginia and daughter Kathy had succumbed to the plague before it was widely known by the public that the dead would return to life. Instead of taking his wife to the same public burn pit used to dispose of his daughter's corpse, Morgan buried her without the knowledge of the authorities. When his wife returned to his home and attacked him, Morgan became aware of the need to kill the plague victims with a wooden stake. Morgan hypothesizes that he is [immune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunity_\(medicine\) "Immunity (medicine)") to the [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria") from a bite by an infected [vampire bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire_bat "Vampire bat") when he was stationed in [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), which may have introduced a diluted form of the plague into his blood.

One day, a dog appears in the neighborhood. Desperate for companionship, Morgan chases after the dog, but does not catch it. Sometime later the dog appears, wounded, at Morgan's doorstep. He takes the dog into his home and treats its wounds, looking forward to having company for the first time in three years. He quickly discovers, however, that it, too, has become infected with the plague. Morgan starts burying the dog, which is now impaled with a wooden stake. He sinks further into depression and loneliness.

After burying the dog, Morgan spots a woman in the distance. The woman, Ruth, is terrified of Morgan at first sight and runs from him. Morgan convinces her to return to his home, but he is suspicious of her true nature. Ruth becomes ill when Morgan waves garlic in her face, but claims that she has a weak stomach. Morgan's suspicion that Ruth is infected is confirmed when he discovers her attempting to inject herself with a combination of blood and [vaccine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccine "Vaccine") that holds the disease at bay. Ruth initially draws a gun on Morgan, but ultimately surrenders it to him. She tells him that she is part of a group of people like her — infected, but under treatment — and was sent to spy on Morgan. The vaccine allows the people to function normally with the drug in the bloodstream, but once it wears off, the infection takes over the body again. Ruth explains that her people are planning to rebuild society as they destroy the remaining humans, and that many of the vampires Morgan killed were still alive. Ruth desperately urges Morgan to flee, but he refuses.

While Ruth is asleep, Morgan transfuses his own blood into her. She is immediately cured, and Morgan sees hope that, together, they can cure the rest of her people. Moments later, however, Ruth's people attack. Morgan takes the gun and flees his home while the attackers kill the vampires gathered around Morgan's home. Ruth's people spot Morgan and chase him. He exchanges gunfire with them and picks up [tear gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tear_gas "Tear gas") grenades from a police station armory along the way. While the tear gas delays his pursuers somewhat, Morgan is wounded by gunfire and retreats into a church. As he stands at the [altar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar "Altar"), Morgan denounces his pursuers as "freaks" and one of his pursuers finally impales him with a thrown spear. In his final moments as Ruth cradles him, Morgan laments that his pursuers were afraid of him, then declares that he is the last true man on Earth, before bleeding out. As Ruth walks away from Morgan's body, she notices a baby crying and tries to assure the child that everyone is safe now.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")\]

Producer [Anthony Hinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hinds "Anthony Hinds") purchased the rights to Matheson's novel for [Hammer Film Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammer_Film_Productions "Hammer Film Productions"). Matheson wrote a script, and Hammer announced in 1958 that they would make it.[\[3\]](#cite_note-4) However, [British censors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_censorship_in_the_United_Kingdom "Film censorship in the United Kingdom") would not allow the film to be produced, so Hinds resold the script to American producer [Robert L. Lippert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_L._Lippert "Robert L. Lippert").

Lippert had wanted to make a "last man on Earth"-type film for a while. In the late 1950s, [Charles Marquis Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Marquis_Warren "Charles Marquis Warren") and Robert Stabler optioned a novel by science fiction writer [George R. Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_R._Stewart "George R. Stewart") called *[Earth Abides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_Abides "Earth Abides")*. [Harry Spalding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Spalding "Harry Spalding"), who worked for Lippert, said the release of *[The World, the Flesh and the Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World,_the_Flesh_and_the_Devil_\(1959_film\) "The World, the Flesh and the Devil (1959 film)")* (1959) killed off plans for that project. Spalding then read Matheson's novel and suggested Lippert film that book instead.[\[4\]](#cite_note-harry-5) The project was announced in August 1962\.

Lippert originally told Matheson that [Fritz Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Lang "Fritz Lang") would direct the film, and Matheson thought that would be "wonderful". Eventually, however, [Sidney Salkow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Salkow "Sidney Salkow") was chosen to direct. Matheson made the follow-up comment: "Well, there's a bit of a drop."[\[5\]](#cite_note-tom-6)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Filming")\]

To save money, the film was shot in [black and white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_and_white "Black and white") in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy") with a predominantly Italian cast and crew.[\[6\]](#cite_note-AIP-7)[\[7\]](#cite_note-8) [Vincent Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Price "Vincent Price") and child actress Christi Courtland were the only Americans among the cast. Typically for an Italian production of the time, the film was shot [MOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOS_\(filmmaking\) "MOS (filmmaking)") (without sync sound). The Italian cast recited their English dialogue [phonetically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonetics "Phonetics"), and were later [dubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubbing "Dubbing") by English-speaking voice actors. [Franca Bettoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franca_Bettoia "Franca Bettoia") was dubbed by [Carolyn De Fonseca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolyn_De_Fonseca "Carolyn De Fonseca").

Much of the film was shot on the futuristic architecture of the [EUR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EUR,_Rome "EUR, Rome") district. Interiors were shot on sets at the [Titanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanus "Titanus") studios. The climax was shot in [San Pio X alla Balduina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Pio_X_alla_Balduina "San Pio X alla Balduina"), a Catholic church in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").[\[8\]](#cite_note-9)[\[9\]](#cite_note-10)[\[10\]](#cite_note-auto-11)

Matheson later said the film was the most faithful adaptation of his book, but he also called the result "inept" and used a pen name for his screenplay. He later said he thought [Harrison Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison_Ford "Harrison Ford") as star and [George Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Miller_\(filmmaker\) "George Miller (filmmaker)") as director would have been the ideal creative combination.[\[5\]](#cite_note-tom-6)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Release")\]

The film was released in the United States by [American International Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_International_Pictures "American International Pictures") on May 6, 1964\. A dubbed version was released in Rome in 1964\.

## Home media

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Home media")\]

[MGM Home Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer"), the current owners of the AIP film catalog, released a digitally remastered [widescreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widescreen "Widescreen") version of the film on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD-Video "DVD-Video") in September 2005\. In 2014, Scream Factory released Blu-ray version in the Vince Price Collection II, which included six other Vincent Price films.

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reception")\]

Although the film was not considered a success upon its release, it later gained a more favorable reputation as a classic of the genre.[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-12) As of February 2025, *The Last Man on Earth* holds an 80% rating at the film [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") Web site [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") from 30 reviews.[\[12\]](#cite_note-13) [Phil Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Hall_\(US_writer\) "Phil Hall (US writer)") of *[Film Threat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_Threat "Film Threat")* called *The Last Man on Earth* "the best Vincent Price movie ever made".[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-12)

Among the less favorable reviews, Steve Biodrowski of *[Cinefantastique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinefantastique "Cinefantastique")* felt the film was "hampered by an obviously low budget and some poorly recorded, post-production dubbing that creates an amateurish feel, undermining the power of its story",[\[13\]](#cite_note-cinefantastique-14) while [Jonathan Rosenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Rosenbaum "Jonathan Rosenbaum") of the *[Chicago Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Reader "Chicago Reader")* remarked, "Some would consider this version better than the 1971 [remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remake "Remake") with [Charlton Heston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlton_Heston "Charlton Heston"), *[The Omega Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Omega_Man "The Omega Man")*, but that isn't much of an achievement".[\[14\]](#cite_note-15)

### Creators' response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Creators' response")\]

Among the film's creators, Price "had a certain fondness for the film" and felt it was better than *The Omega Man*.[\[13\]](#cite_note-cinefantastique-14)

Richard Matheson co-wrote the film's screenplay, but was unhappy with the results. To keep receiving [residual income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_income "Passive income") from the film, though, he had to be credited, so he used the name "Logan Swanson", a combination of his wife's mother's maiden name and his mother's maiden name.[\[15\]](#cite_note-16) Matheson said: "I was disappointed in the film, even though they more or less followed my story. I think Vincent Price, whom I love in every one of his pictures that I wrote, was miscast. I also felt the direction was kind of poor. I just didn't care for it."[\[16\]](#cite_note-17)

***The Last Man on Earth*** ([Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language"): ***L'ultimo uomo della Terra***) is a 1964 [post-apocalyptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocalyptic_and_post-apocalyptic_fiction "Apocalyptic and post-apocalyptic fiction") [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction_film "Science fiction film") [horror film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_film "Horror film") directed by [Sidney Salkow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Salkow "Sidney Salkow") and [Ubaldo Ragona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubaldo_Ragona "Ubaldo Ragona"), based on the 1954 novel *[I Am Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Legend_\(novel\) "I Am Legend (novel)")* by [Richard Matheson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Matheson "Richard Matheson"). It stars [Vincent Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Price "Vincent Price") and [Franca Bettoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franca_Bettoia "Franca Bettoia"), and was produced by [Robert L. Lippert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_L._Lippert "Robert L. Lippert"). The screenplay was written in part by Matheson, but he was dissatisfied with the result and chose to be credited under the alias "Logan Swanson".

The film was a co-production between the United States and Italy, and was filmed on-location in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"). It was released in the United States by [American International Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_International_Pictures "American International Pictures"). In the 1980s, the film entered the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain").[\[1\]](#cite_note-2)[\[2\]](#cite_note-3)

*The Last Man on Earth* is the first of three adaptations of Matheson's novel, followed by *[The Omega Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Omega_Man "The Omega Man")* (1971) and [*I Am Legend*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Legend_\(film\) "I Am Legend (film)") (2007).

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*The Last Man on Earth* (full movie)

It is 1968, and Dr. Robert Morgan lives in a world where everyone else has been infected by a [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemic "Pandemic") that has turned them into [undead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undead "Undead"), [vampiric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire") creatures that cannot stand sunlight, fear mirrors, and are repelled by [garlic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic "Garlic"). They would kill Morgan if they could, but they are weak and unintelligent. Every day Morgan carries out the same routine: He wakes up, marks another day on the calendar, gathers his weapons, and then goes hunting for [vampires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire "Vampire"), killing as many as he can and then burning the bodies to prevent them from coming back. At night, he locks himself inside his house.

A [flashback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashback_\(narrative\) "Flashback (narrative)") sequence explains that, in December 1965, Morgan's wife Virginia and daughter Kathy had succumbed to the plague before it was widely known by the public that the dead would return to life. Instead of taking his wife to the same public burn pit used to dispose of his daughter's corpse, Morgan buried her without the knowledge of the authorities. When his wife returned to his home and attacked him, Morgan became aware of the need to kill the plague victims with a wooden stake. Morgan hypothesizes that he is [immune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunity_\(medicine\) "Immunity (medicine)") to the [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria") from a bite by an infected [vampire bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire_bat "Vampire bat") when he was stationed in [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), which may have introduced a diluted form of the plague into his blood.

One day, a dog appears in the neighborhood. Desperate for companionship, Morgan chases after the dog, but does not catch it. Sometime later the dog appears, wounded, at Morgan's doorstep. He takes the dog into his home and treats its wounds, looking forward to having company for the first time in three years. He quickly discovers, however, that it, too, has become infected with the plague. Morgan starts burying the dog, which is now impaled with a wooden stake. He sinks further into depression and loneliness.

After burying the dog, Morgan spots a woman in the distance. The woman, Ruth, is terrified of Morgan at first sight and runs from him. Morgan convinces her to return to his home, but he is suspicious of her true nature. Ruth becomes ill when Morgan waves garlic in her face, but claims that she has a weak stomach. Morgan's suspicion that Ruth is infected is confirmed when he discovers her attempting to inject herself with a combination of blood and [vaccine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccine "Vaccine") that holds the disease at bay. Ruth initially draws a gun on Morgan, but ultimately surrenders it to him. She tells him that she is part of a group of people like her — infected, but under treatment — and was sent to spy on Morgan. The vaccine allows the people to function normally with the drug in the bloodstream, but once it wears off, the infection takes over the body again. Ruth explains that her people are planning to rebuild society as they destroy the remaining humans, and that many of the vampires Morgan killed were still alive. Ruth desperately urges Morgan to flee, but he refuses.

While Ruth is asleep, Morgan transfuses his own blood into her. She is immediately cured, and Morgan sees hope that, together, they can cure the rest of her people. Moments later, however, Ruth's people attack. Morgan takes the gun and flees his home while the attackers kill the vampires gathered around Morgan's home. Ruth's people spot Morgan and chase him. He exchanges gunfire with them and picks up [tear gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tear_gas "Tear gas") grenades from a police station armory along the way. While the tear gas delays his pursuers somewhat, Morgan is wounded by gunfire and retreats into a church. As he stands at the [altar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar "Altar"), Morgan denounces his pursuers as "freaks" and one of his pursuers finally impales him with a thrown spear. In his final moments as Ruth cradles him, Morgan laments that his pursuers were afraid of him, then declares that he is the last true man on Earth, before bleeding out. As Ruth walks away from Morgan's body, she notices a baby crying and tries to assure the child that everyone is safe now.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")\]

Producer [Anthony Hinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hinds "Anthony Hinds") purchased the rights to Matheson's novel for [Hammer Film Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammer_Film_Productions "Hammer Film Productions"). Matheson wrote a script, and Hammer announced in 1958 that they would make it.[\[3\]](#cite_note-4) However, [British censors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_censorship_in_the_United_Kingdom "Film censorship in the United Kingdom") would not allow the film to be produced, so Hinds resold the script to American producer [Robert L. Lippert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_L._Lippert "Robert L. Lippert").

Lippert had wanted to make a "last man on Earth"-type film for a while. In the late 1950s, [Charles Marquis Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Marquis_Warren "Charles Marquis Warren") and Robert Stabler optioned a novel by science fiction writer [George R. Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_R._Stewart "George R. Stewart") called *[Earth Abides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_Abides "Earth Abides")*. [Harry Spalding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Spalding "Harry Spalding"), who worked for Lippert, said the release of *[The World, the Flesh and the Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World,_the_Flesh_and_the_Devil_\(1959_film\) "The World, the Flesh and the Devil (1959 film)")* (1959) killed off plans for that project. Spalding then read Matheson's novel and suggested Lippert film that book instead.[\[4\]](#cite_note-harry-5) The project was announced in August 1962\.

Lippert originally told Matheson that [Fritz Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Lang "Fritz Lang") would direct the film, and Matheson thought that would be "wonderful". Eventually, however, [Sidney Salkow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Salkow "Sidney Salkow") was chosen to direct. Matheson made the follow-up comment: "Well, there's a bit of a drop."[\[5\]](#cite_note-tom-6)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Filming")\]

To save money, the film was shot in [black and white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_and_white "Black and white") in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy") with a predominantly Italian cast and crew.[\[6\]](#cite_note-AIP-7)[\[7\]](#cite_note-8) [Vincent Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Price "Vincent Price") and child actress Christi Courtland were the only Americans among the cast. Typically for an Italian production of the time, the film was shot [MOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOS_\(filmmaking\) "MOS (filmmaking)") (without sync sound). The Italian cast recited their English dialogue [phonetically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonetics "Phonetics"), and were later [dubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubbing "Dubbing") by English-speaking voice actors. [Franca Bettoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franca_Bettoia "Franca Bettoia") was dubbed by [Carolyn De Fonseca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolyn_De_Fonseca "Carolyn De Fonseca").

Much of the film was shot on the futuristic architecture of the [EUR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EUR,_Rome "EUR, Rome") district. Interiors were shot on sets at the [Titanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanus "Titanus") studios. The climax was shot in [San Pio X alla Balduina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Pio_X_alla_Balduina "San Pio X alla Balduina"), a Catholic church in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").[\[8\]](#cite_note-9)[\[9\]](#cite_note-10)[\[10\]](#cite_note-auto-11)

Matheson later said the film was the most faithful adaptation of his book, but he also called the result "inept" and used a pen name for his screenplay. He later said he thought [Harrison Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison_Ford "Harrison Ford") as star and [George Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Miller_\(filmmaker\) "George Miller (filmmaker)") as director would have been the ideal creative combination.[\[5\]](#cite_note-tom-6)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Release")\]

The film was released in the United States by [American International Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_International_Pictures "American International Pictures") on May 6, 1964\. A dubbed version was released in Rome in 1964\.

## Home media

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Home media")\]

[MGM Home Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer"), the current owners of the AIP film catalog, released a digitally remastered [widescreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widescreen "Widescreen") version of the film on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD-Video "DVD-Video") in September 2005\. In 2014, Scream Factory released Blu-ray version in the Vince Price Collection II, which included six other Vincent Price films.

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reception")\]

Although the film was not considered a success upon its release, it later gained a more favorable reputation as a classic of the genre.[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-12) As of February 2025, *The Last Man on Earth* holds an 80% rating at the film [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") Web site [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") from 30 reviews.[\[12\]](#cite_note-13) [Phil Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Hall_\(US_writer\) "Phil Hall (US writer)") of *[Film Threat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_Threat "Film Threat")* called *The Last Man on Earth* "the best Vincent Price movie ever made".[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-12)

Among the less favorable reviews, Steve Biodrowski of *[Cinefantastique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinefantastique "Cinefantastique")* felt the film was "hampered by an obviously low budget and some poorly recorded, post-production dubbing that creates an amateurish feel, undermining the power of its story",[\[13\]](#cite_note-cinefantastique-14) while [Jonathan Rosenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Rosenbaum "Jonathan Rosenbaum") of the *[Chicago Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Reader "Chicago Reader")* remarked, "Some would consider this version better than the 1971 [remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remake "Remake") with [Charlton Heston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlton_Heston "Charlton Heston"), *[The Omega Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Omega_Man "The Omega Man")*, but that isn't much of an achievement".[\[14\]](#cite_note-15)

### Creators' response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Last_Man_on_Earth_\(1964_film\)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Creators' response")\]

Among the film's creators, Price "had a certain fondness for the film" and felt it was better than *The Omega Man*.[\[13\]](#cite_note-cinefantastique-14)

Richard Matheson co-wrote the film's screenplay, but was unhappy with the results. To keep receiving [residual income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_income "Passive income") from the film, though, he had to be credited, so he used the name "Logan Swanson", a combination of his wife's mother's maiden name and his mother's maiden name.[\[15\]](#cite_note-16) Matheson said: "I was disappointed in the film, even though they more or less followed my story. I think Vincent Price, whom I love in every one of his pictures that I wrote, was miscast. I also felt the direction was kind of poor. I just didn't care for it."[\[16\]](#cite_note-17)

The Wikipedia plot summary confirms the film's day/night structure. My analysis is complete — here's the full reasoning:

## Analysis

**1. The barcode is pure grayscale, ~1000 one-pixel stripes** (measured: 1000×200 px, ~980 independent columns). If each stripe is ~5 seconds, the runtime is ≈ 83 minutes — consistent with a feature like *The Last Man on Earth* (86 min → 5.2 s/stripe, a textbook "few seconds").

**2. No intertitles → sound film.** The brightest stripe in the whole image is only 143/255, and zero stripes exceed 150. Silent films (*Joan of Arc*, *The Kid*, *Potemkin*, *Metropolis*) would produce near-white stripes wherever a title card fills several seconds. Also, *Joan of Arc* is famously high-key (bright white backdrops), as are *His Girl Friday* and *The Lady Vanishes* — their barcodes would average far above 57 and contain many bright stripes. All ruled out.

**3. The luminance timeline matches one film's structure almost exactly:**

| Barcode feature | Location | The Last Man on Earth |
|---|---|---|
| Very dark opening (28–37) | 0–5% | Famous night opening: aerial shots of the dead city, radio broadcast, boarded-up house |
| Sudden bright spike (71) | 5–6% | Dawn arrives; day begins |
| Sustained bright plateau (up to 93) | 13–24% | His long **daylight** scavenging routine through Rome's sun-bleached white EUR district, staking sleeping vampires |
| Medium-dark middle (41–61) | 24–60% | Burn pits, the dog, the hospital flashback |
| Bright second region (70–88) | 60–68% | Ruth, daylight scenes after the dog's death |
| Darkest sustained dip (30–41) | 79–84% | The mutants' **night** siege and chase |
| Dark-medium ending with small bright bumps | 84–100% | Night chase → church interior → dawn aftermath |

The other dark candidates fail: *All Quiet*'s 13–24% mark is the black-out night bombardment and first charge at the front (should be darkest, not brightest); *House on Haunted Hill* has no bright mid-film plateau (it gets darker after arriving at the house) and ends in bright daylight, unlike our dark ending; *The Little Shop of Horrors*' corresponding stretch is moody shop interiors, not a 10-minute bright plateau.

The signature of *The Last Man on Earth* is precisely this stark alternation of near-black nights and blazing Mediterranean daylight — which is exactly what this barcode shows.
